verses.13:6: From there he ordered the sacrilegious man to be thrown down into the ashes, while all pushed him forward to destruction.
verses.13:7: And by such a law it happened that the transgressor of the law died, and Menelaus was not given to the earth.
verses.13:8: And indeed justly enough; for because he committed many offenses against the altar of God, whose fire and ashes were holy, he himself was condemned to a death of ashes.
verses.13:9: But the king was coming, unbridled in mind, intending to show himself to the Jews more wicked than his father.
verses.13:10: When Judas learned of these things, he commanded the people to call upon the Lord day and night, so that, as always, He might help them now also,
verses.13:11: since indeed they feared being deprived of the law, their homeland, and the holy temple; and so that He would not allow the people, who had recently caught their breath a little, to be subjected again to blasphemous nations.
verses.13:12: Therefore, while all did this together and sought mercy from the Lord with weeping and fasts, lying prostrate for three continuous days, Judas urged them to prepare themselves.
verses.13:13: And he himself, together with the elders, resolved, before the king brought his army up to Judea and took possession of the city, to go out and commit the outcome of the matter to the judgment of the Lord.
verses.13:14: Therefore, giving authority over all things to God, the Creator of the world, and having urged his men to fight bravely and to stand even to death for the laws, the temple, the city, the homeland, and the citizens, he stationed the army around Modin.
verses.13:15: And having given his men the watchword of God's victory, with the bravest young men chosen, he attacked the royal pavilion by night and killed four thousand men in the camp, and the largest of the elephants along with those who had been placed upon it;
verses.13:16: and filling the camp of the enemies with the greatest fear and confusion, having carried out their undertaking successfully, they departed.
verses.13:17: And this took place as day was dawning, with the protection of the Lord helping him.
verses.13:18: But the king, having received a taste of the boldness of the Jews, tested the difficulty of the terrain by stratagem,
verses.13:19: and moved his camp up to Beth-zur, which was a fortified stronghold of the Jews; but he was driven back, he stumbled, he was diminished.
verses.13:20: And Judas kept sending necessities to those who were inside.
verses.13:21: But a certain Rhodocus from the Jewish army disclosed secrets to the enemies; when tracked down, he was seized and imprisoned.
verses.13:22: Again the king held talks with those who were in Beth-zur; he gave the right hand, received it, departed;
verses.13:23: he engaged Judas in battle, and was defeated. But when he learned that Philip, who had been left over affairs, had rebelled in Antioch, dismayed in mind, appealing to the Jews and yielding to them, he swore concerning all things that seemed just; and having been reconciled, he offered a sacrifice, honored the temple, and presented gifts.
verses.13:24: He embraced Maccabeus and made him commander and ruler from Ptolemais to the Gerrenians.
verses.13:25: But when he came to Ptolemais, the people of Ptolemais took the agreement of friendship badly, being indignant, for fear that perhaps they might violate the covenant.
verses.13:26: Then Lysias ascended the tribunal, and explained the reason, and calmed the people, and returned to Antioch; and in this way the king's departure and return proceeded.
verses.14:1: But after a period of three years, Judas and those who were with him learned that Demetrius, son of Seleucus, had gone up with a strong multitude and ships through the gate of Tripolis to advantageous places,
verses.14:2: and had occupied the regions against Antiochus and his commander Lysias.
verses.14:3: Now a certain Alcimus, who had been high priest, but had voluntarily defiled himself during the times of mingling, considering that in no way was there safety for him nor access to the altar,
verses.14:4: came to King Demetrius in the one hundred and fiftieth year, offering him a golden crown and a palm, and in addition to these also boughs that seemed to belong to the temple. And on that very day he kept silent.
verses.14:5: But having found an opportune time for his madness, when he was summoned by Demetrius to the council and asked on what things and plans the Jews relied,
verses.14:6: he answered, "Those very ones among the Jews who are called Hasideans, whom Judas Maccabeus leads, foster wars and stir up seditions, and do not allow the kingdom to be tranquil;
verses.14:7: for I myself also, defrauded of the glory of my ancestors (I mean the high priesthood), have come here:
verses.14:8: first indeed keeping faith with the interests of the king, and second also looking out for the citizens; for by their wickedness our entire nation is harassed in no small measure.
verses.14:9: But I beg you, king, once each of these matters is known, provide for both the region and the nation, according to your kindness that is widely known to all;
verses.14:10: for as long as Judas survives, it is impossible for affairs to be at peace."
verses.14:11: Now when such things had been spoken by him, the rest of the friends also, being hostilely disposed toward Judas, inflamed Demetrius.
verses.14:12: He immediately sent Nicanor, who was in charge of the elephants, into Judea as commander,
verses.14:13: having given orders that he should capture Judas himself, but scatter those who were with him, and appoint Alcimus as high priest of the greatest temple.
verses.14:14: Then the Gentiles who had fled from Judas out of Judea joined themselves to Nicanor in droves, considering the miseries and disasters of the Jews to be the prosperity of their own affairs.
verses.14:15: Therefore, when the Jews heard of the arrival of Nicanor and the assembly of the nations, sprinkled with earth, they pleaded with Him who established His people to guard them forever, and who protects His own portion with evident signs.
verses.14:16: Now when the commander gave the order, they immediately moved out from there and assembled at the stronghold of Dessau.
verses.14:17: Now Simon, the brother of Judas, had engaged in battle with Nicanor, but he was terrified by the sudden arrival of the adversaries.
verses.14:18: Yet Nicanor, hearing of the valor of the companions of Judas and the greatness of spirit that they had for the struggles of their homeland, was afraid to make the decision by blood.
verses.14:19: For this reason he sent ahead Posidonius, Theodotius, and Matthias, so that they might give and receive right hands.
verses.14:20: And when deliberation had gone on for a long time concerning these matters, and the commander himself had reported it to the multitude, the single decision of all was to agree to friendship.
verses.14:21: Therefore they appointed a day on which they might confer privately with one another; and seats were brought out and placed for each of them.
verses.14:22: Now Judas ordered armed men to be in advantageous places, in case any evil might suddenly arise from the enemies; and they held a fitting conference.
verses.14:23: Now Nicanor stayed in Jerusalem and did nothing unjustly; and he dismissed the throngs of the crowds that had been gathered together.
verses.14:24: Moreover, he always held Judas dear from his heart, and he was inclined toward the man.
verses.14:25: And he asked him to take a wife and father children. He married, lived quietly, and they shared a common life.
verses.14:26: But Alcimus, seeing their affection for one another and their agreements, came to Demetrius and kept saying that Nicanor was assenting to alien interests, and had appointed Judas, a plotter against the kingdom, as his own successor.
verses.14:27: Therefore the king, enraged and provoked by this man's most wicked accusations, wrote to Nicanor, saying that he was indeed gravely displeased over the agreement of friendship, yet that he commanded him to send Maccabeus bound to Antioch quickly.
verses.14:28: When he learned of these things, Nicanor was dismayed and was gravely distressed if he should make void the things that had been agreed upon, having been wronged in nothing by the man;
verses.14:29: but because he could not resist the king, he watched for an opportunity by which he might carry out the command.
verses.14:30: But Maccabeus, seeing that Nicanor was dealing more sternly with him and conducting their customary meetings more roughly, and understanding that this sternness came from no good, having gathered a few of his own men, hid himself from Nicanor.
verses.14:31: When he recognized this, that he had been boldly forestalled by the man, he came to the greatest and most holy temple; and while the priests were offering the customary sacrifices, he ordered the man to be handed over to him.
verses.14:32: When they declared with an oath that they did not know where the one who was being sought was, stretching out his hand toward the temple,
verses.14:33: he swore, saying, "Unless you hand Judas over to me bound, I will bring this sanctuary of God down to level ground, and I will dig up the altar, and I will consecrate this temple to Father Liber."
verses.14:34: And having said these things, he departed. But the priests, stretching out their hands toward heaven, called upon Him who was always the defender of their nation, saying these words:
verses.14:35: "You, Lord of all things, who have need of nothing, have willed that the temple of Your dwelling be made among us.
verses.14:36: And now, Holy One of holies, Lord of all, preserve forever undefiled this house that was recently cleansed."
verses.14:37: Now a certain Razis, one of the elders from Jerusalem, was denounced to Nicanor, a man who was a lover of the city and well spoken of, who because of his affection was called the father of the Jews.
verses.14:38: For a long time this man maintained a resolve of self-restraint in Judaism, and was content to surrender body and soul for perseverance.
verses.14:39: Now Nicanor, wanting to display the hatred that he had against the Jews, sent five hundred soldiers to seize him.
verses.14:40: For he thought that if he ensnared him, he would inflict the greatest disaster upon the Jews.
verses.14:41: Now while the crowds were eager to rush into his house, break down the door, and apply fire to it, since he was now about to be seized, he struck at himself with a sword,
verses.14:42: choosing to die nobly rather than become subject to sinners and be treated with unworthy outrages contrary to his birth.
verses.14:43: But because in his haste he had not dealt the wound with a sure stroke, and the crowds were bursting inside the doors, running back boldly to the wall, he threw himself headlong manfully into the crowds;
verses.14:44: and as they quickly gave way to his fall, he came down on the middle of his neck.
verses.14:45: And while he was still breathing, inflamed in spirit, he stood up; and although his blood was flowing down in a great stream and he was stricken with the most severe wounds, he passed through the crowd at a run;
verses.14:46: and standing upon a certain steep rock, and having now become drained of blood, grasping his own intestines, he threw them with both hands upon the crowds, calling upon the Sovereign of life and spirit that He would restore these to him again; and thus he departed from life.
verses.15:1: Now Nicanor, when he learned that Judas was in the regions of Samaria, planned to engage in battle with all force on the Sabbath day.
verses.15:2: And when the Jews who were following him under compulsion said, "Do not act so savagely and barbarously, but pay honor to the day of sanctification, and honor Him who sees all things,"
verses.15:3: that wretched man asked whether there is a mighty one in heaven who commanded the Sabbath day to be observed.
verses.15:4: And when they answered, "There is the living Lord Himself, mighty in heaven, who ordered the seventh day to be observed,"
verses.15:5: he in turn said, "I also am mighty on the earth, I who command arms to be taken up and the king's affairs to be fulfilled." Yet he did not succeed in completing his plan.
verses.15:6: And Nicanor indeed, lifted up with the utmost pride, had planned to set up a public trophy over Judas.
verses.15:7: But Maccabeus was always confident, with every hope that help from God would come to him;
verses.15:8: and he exhorted his men not to be afraid at the approach of the nations, but to keep in mind the acts of help done for them from heaven, and now to hope that victory would come to them from the Almighty.
verses.15:9: And addressing them from the Law and the Prophets, reminding them also of the struggles that they had fought before, he made them more eager;
verses.15:10: and thus, with their spirits lifted up, he at the same time showed the deceit of the Gentiles and the violation of oaths.
verses.15:11: Now he armed each one of them, not with the protection of shield and spear, but with excellent words and exhortations, after relating a dream worthy of belief, through which he gladdened all of them.
verses.15:12: Now the vision was of this kind: Onias, who had been high priest, a good and kind man, modest in appearance, gentle in conduct, and dignified in speech, and one who from boyhood had been trained in virtues, was stretching out his hands, praying for the entire people of the Jews.
verses.15:13: After this, another man also appeared, remarkable in age and glory, and with a bearing of great dignity around him.
verses.15:14: And Onias answered and said, "This is the lover of the brothers and of the people of Israel; this is the one who prays much for the people and the entire holy city, Jeremiah, the prophet of God."
verses.15:15: Then Jeremiah stretched out his right hand and gave Judas a golden sword, saying,
verses.15:16: "Take the holy sword, a gift from God, with which you will cast down the adversaries of my people Israel."
verses.15:17: Encouraged therefore by the very good words of Judas, by which ardor could be raised up and the spirits of the young men strengthened, they resolved to fight and to engage bravely, so that valor might decide the affairs, because the holy city and the temple were in danger.
verses.15:18: For there was less anxiety for wives and children, and likewise for brothers and relatives; but the greatest and foremost fear was for the holiness of the temple.
verses.15:19: Moreover, no small anxiety gripped those also who were in the city for those who were about to engage in battle.
verses.15:20: And when all were now expecting the coming judgment, and the enemies were at hand and the army was drawn up in order, with the beasts and horsemen stationed in an advantageous place,
verses.15:21: Maccabeus, observing the approach of the multitude, and the varied array of arms, and the fierceness of the beasts, stretching out his hands toward heaven, called upon the Lord who works wonders, who, not according to the power of arms, but just as it pleases Him, gives victory to the worthy.
verses.15:22: And calling upon Him, he spoke in this manner: "You, Lord, who sent Your angel under Hezekiah king of Judah, and killed one hundred eighty-five thousand from the camp of Sennacherib,
verses.15:23: and now, Sovereign of the heavens, send Your good angel before us in fear and trembling at the greatness of Your arm,
verses.15:24: so that those who come with blasphemy against Your holy people may be afraid." And he indeed concluded his plea in this way.
verses.15:25: Now Nicanor and those who were with him were advancing with trumpets and songs.
verses.15:26: But Judas and those who were with him, having called upon God, engaged in battle through prayers:
verses.15:27: fighting indeed by hand, yet praying to the Lord in their hearts, they struck down no fewer than thirty-five thousand, greatly delighted by the presence of God.
verses.15:28: And when they had finished and were returning with joy, they discovered that Nicanor had fallen in his armor.
verses.15:29: Therefore, when a shout was raised and a commotion was stirred up, they blessed the Almighty Lord in their native tongue.
verses.15:30: Now Judas, who in every way was ready in body and soul to die for the citizens, commanded that the head of Nicanor, and his hand cut off with the shoulder, be carried to Jerusalem.
verses.15:31: When he arrived there, having called together his fellow tribesmen and the priests to the altar, he summoned also those who were in the citadel.
verses.15:32: And after showing the head of Nicanor, and the wicked hand which he had stretched out against the holy house of Almighty God as he boasted grandly,
verses.15:33: he also ordered the tongue of the impious Nicanor to be cut off and given piece by piece to the birds, and the hand of the madman to be hung opposite the temple.
verses.15:34: Therefore all the heavens blessed the Lord, saying, "Blessed is He who has preserved His own place undefiled."
verses.15:35: And he hung the head of Nicanor at the top of the citadel, so that it might be an evident and unmistakable sign of the help of God.
verses.15:36: Therefore all of them decreed by common consent in no way to let that day pass without celebration.
verses.15:37: Rather, they were to hold a celebration on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, as it is called in the Syriac tongue, the day before Mordecai's day.
verses.15:38: So, with these matters concerning Nicanor accomplished, and the city having been possessed by the Hebrews from those times, I also will make an end of the account at this point.
verses.15:39: And if indeed it is well done, and as befits a history, this is what I myself would wish; but if less worthily, allowance must be made for me.
verses.15:40: For just as always drinking wine, or always water, is harmful, while using them in turn is delightful, so for readers, if the account is always exacting, it will not be pleasing. Here, therefore, it will be completed.

notes.1:12: The Vulgate reads 'ebullire fecit de Perside' ("caused to pour forth from Persia") regarding those who fought against Jerusalem, whereas the Greek Septuagint reads "cast out those who arrayed themselves in the holy city" without mentioning Persia.
notes.1:21: The Vulgate reads nominative 'sacerdos Nehemias' ("the priest Nehemiah"), whereas the Greek Septuagint has Nehemiah commanding "the priests" to sprinkle the sacrifices.
notes.1:24: The Vulgate retains third-person 'qui solus est bonus rex' ("who alone is a good King") within second-person address, rendering the Greek substantival phrase for "the only good King."
notes.1:34: The Vulgate reads 'fecit ei templum, ut probaret quod factum erat' ("made a temple for it in order to verify what had happened"), whereas the Greek Septuagint states that the king enclosed the site and made it sacred.
notes.1:36: The Vulgate specifies 'hunc locum' ("this place") rather than the thick liquid itself, and preserves the distinct popular name 'Nephi' (Greek 'Nephthai').
notes.2:8: The Vulgate reads 'magno Deo' ("to the great God") and adds 'manifestabat haec' ("He manifested these things"), whereas the Greek Septuagint has the adverb "greatly" without the final clause.
notes.2:9: The Vulgate reads 'Magnifice etenim sapientiam tractabat' ("For indeed he practiced wisdom magnificently"), whereas the Greek Septuagint states, "It was also explained that, having wisdom..."
notes.2:13: The Vulgate reads 'de regionibus' ("from the regions") where the Greek Septuagint refers to books "about the kings."
notes.2:18: The Clementine Vulgate reads the perfect 'congregavit' ("has gathered," likely an early b/v spelling variant for future 'congregabit', "will gather," as in the Greek); the continuation ('For He has rescued us...') follows in native 2:19.
notes.2:19: Native Vulgate 2 Maccabees 2:19 maps to Saints.Bible 2:18b (shifting native 2:20-33 to Saints.Bible 2:19-32).
notes.2:21: The Vulgate translates the royal epithet 'Epiphanes' as 'Nobilem' ("the Noble"), and in v. 22 renders Greek 'epiphaneias' ("manifestations") as 'illuminationibus' ("illuminations").
notes.3:4: The Vulgate states that Simon strove 'to contrive something unjust in the city' (iniquum aliquid in civitate moliri), whereas the Greek describes a dispute with the high priest over the administration of the city market.
notes.3:5: The Latin reads Tharsææ ('of Tharseas'), matching the Greek manuscripts' Tharseou; some modern editions of the Greek emend the name to 'Thraseas.'
notes.3:11: The Vulgate reads positively 'among the things that the impious Simon had reported' (in his quæ detulerat impius Simon), whereas the Greek Septuagint explicitly denies Simon's claim ('not at all as the impious Simon had slanderously represented').
notes.3:19: The Vulgate reads that the secluded virgins ran out 'to Onias' (ad Oniam), whereas the Greek Septuagint reads 'to the gates'.
notes.3:24: The Vulgate reads 'the Spirit of Almighty God' (spiritus omnipotentis Dei), whereas the Greek Septuagint reads 'the Sovereign of spirits and of all authority'.
notes.4:7: The Vulgate translates Antiochus IV's Greek epithet Epiphanes ("Illustrious") into Latin as Nobilis ("the Noble").
notes.4:12: The Vulgate reads in lupanaribus ("in brothels"), whereas the Greek Septuagint reads hypo petason ("under the petasos," the broad-brimmed Greek hat associated with the gymnasium).
notes.4:19: The Vulgate reads viros peccatores ("sinful men") carrying three hundred didrachmas of silver, whereas the Greek describes them as envoys (Antiochenes from Jerusalem) carrying three hundred drachmas.
notes.4:29: The Vulgate states that Menelaus was removed from the priesthood with Lysimachus succeeding him and that Sostratus was placed over the Cyprians, whereas the Greek has Menelaus leaving Lysimachus as deputy and Sostratus leaving Crates, commander of the Cyprians.
notes.4:40: The Vulgate reads duce quodam tyranno ("with a certain tyrant as leader"), whereas the Greek Septuagint has the proper name Auranus.
notes.5:3: The Vulgate reads galeatorum ("of helmeted men"), whereas the Greek Septuagint reads kamaton ("of spear-shafts").
notes.5:14: The Vulgate reads vincti ("bound"), differing from the Greek Septuagint, which describes forty thousand killed in hand-to-hand combat.
notes.5:23: The Vulgate groups Menelaus together with Andronicus at Gerizim with a plural verb (imminebant), whereas the Greek Septuagint separates Menelaus from Andronicus at Gerizim.
notes.5:24: The Vulgate renders Greek mysarchen ("commander of the Mysians") as odiosum principem ("the hateful commander").
notes.5:27: Latin qui decimus fuerat ("who had been the tenth") literally translates a Greek idiom meaning Judas withdrew with about nine others, forming a band of ten.
notes.6:1: The Vulgate reads senem quemdam Antiochenum ("a certain old man from Antioch"), whereas the Greek Septuagint refers to an Athenian elder or senator.
notes.6:2: Here and in 6:7, the Vulgate uses the Roman divine names Jupiter (Jovis) and Liber (Liberi) where the Greek Septuagint has Zeus and Dionysus.
notes.6:14: The clause cum judicii dies advenerit ("when the day of judgment arrives") is a Vulgate-distinct reading absent from the Greek Septuagint; the opening negative Non enim governs ita et in nobis statuit in 6:15.
notes.6:20: The Vulgate wording ("considering how he ought to come forward...") diverges notably from the Greek Septuagint, which states that Eleazar spat out the meat before advancing.
notes.6:21: The Vulgate reads iniqua miseratione commoti ("moved by unjust pity"), where the Greek Septuagint describes those in charge of the unlawful sacrificial meal.
notes.7:5: The Vulgate reads "he ordered fire to be brought near" (ignem admoveri) and "while he was tormented in it for a long time" (in qua cum diu cruciaretur), whereas the Greek Septuagint speaks of bringing him to the fire and of the vapor from the pan spreading widely.
notes.7:6: Latin consolabitur in nobis / in servis suis consolabitur ("will take comfort in us / in His servants") mirrors the Greek passive paraklethesetai ("will have compassion on" or "relent toward") in citing Deuteronomy 32:36; in protestatione cantici ("in the testimony of the song") also renders the Greek ("the song that confronts them face to face") distinctively.
notes.7:20: The Vulgate reads bonorum memoria digna ("worthy of the remembrance of the good"), using the genitive plural bonorum where the Greek Septuagint has "worthy of good remembrance."
notes.7:22: The Vulgate lists three elements, "spirit and soul and life" (spiritum et animam ... et vitam), where the Greek Septuagint mentions only "spirit and life."
notes.7:30: The Vulgate uses the masculine singular interrogative Quem sustinetis? ("Whom are you waiting for?"), resolving the ambiguous Greek tina ("whom" or "what"), and reads "given to us" (nobis) where the Greek has "given to our fathers."
notes.8:8: The Clementine Vulgate reads propere ("swiftly"), whereas some Latin witnesses read prospere ("prosperously"), matching the Greek.
notes.8:16: The Vulgate reads "seven thousand" (septem millibus), whereas the Greek text reads "six thousand," matching 8:1 and the four divisions of 1,500 in 8:22.
notes.8:20: The Vulgate gives the Jewish force as "six thousand" (sex millia) and does not specify the number of Macedonian allies, whereas the Greek reads "eight thousand" Jews alongside "four thousand" Macedonians.
notes.8:23: The Vulgate names "Ezra" (ab Esdra) as the reader of the holy book, whereas the Greek text names "Eleazar."
notes.8:32: The Vulgate treats the Greek title phylarches ("cavalry commander" or "tribal leader") as a proper name, Philarches (accusative Philarchen).
notes.9:19: The Clementine Vulgate reads the plural principes ("princes" or "rulers") alongside Antiochus, whereas the Greek has the singular title strategos ("commander" or "general") referring to Antiochus himself.
notes.9:20: Unlike the Greek text, which adds "to God" (or "to heaven"), the Vulgate simply reads "we give the greatest thanks" (maximas agimus gratias).
notes.9:26: The Latin prints Ora (imperative in form), evidently for Oro ("I implore"), as the parallel first-person et peto ("and ask") and the accusative vos ("you") require.
notes.10:7: The Vulgate omits the Greek reference to offering hymns, making the wreathed staffs (Latin thyrsos, festive staffs entwined with foliage), green branches, and palms the direct objects carried before the Lord.
notes.10:9: "The Noble" renders Latin Nobilis, the Vulgate's translation of the Greek royal epithet Epiphanes (so also in 10:13).
notes.10:12: The Clementine Vulgate gives Ptolemy's surname as Macer, whereas the Greek text reads Macron.
notes.10:15: The Clementine Vulgate reads Judaei ("the Jews"), whereas the Greek Septuagint reads "the Idumeans" (compare 10:16).
notes.10:20: The Vulgate specifies didrachmas (double drachmas), whereas the Greek text has seventy thousand drachmas.
notes.11:5: The Vulgate reads in angusto loco ("in a narrow place"), whereas the Greek describes Beth-zur as a fortified place; both Latin and Greek state five stadia, though Beth-zur lies much farther south of Jerusalem.
notes.11:19: The Clementine Vulgate prints the third-person subjunctive esset ("that there may be a cause of good things for you"), whereas the Greek and some Latin witnesses have the infinitive esse ("to be a cause of good things for you").
notes.11:21: The Vulgate reads the month name Dioscori ("Dioscorus"), corresponding to the obscure Greek name Dioscorinthios, whose exact calendar identification is uncertain.
notes.11:29: Vulgate ad vestros, qui sunt apud nos ("to your own people who are with us") is a distinct Latin reading where the Greek speaks of going down to attend to one's own affairs or homes.
notes.11:36: The Clementine Vulgate prints the infinitive mittere with imperative force ("send"), where some Latin editions read mittite; Vulgate decernamus ("we may decide") also differs from the Greek ("we may explain").
notes.12:11: Latin pascua literally means 'pastures,' whereas the Greek reads boskemata ('livestock' or 'cattle').
notes.12:15: Latin Jesu (reflecting Greek Iesou) refers here to Joshua, son of Nun, under whom the walls of Jericho fell (Josh 6).
notes.12:26: The Vulgate reads simply 'to Carnion' without mentioning the temple of Atargatis (Atargateion) found in the Greek text.
notes.12:41: The Vulgate reads justum judicium Domini ('the righteous judgment of the Lord'), whereas the Greek reads 'the Lord, the righteous judge.'
notes.12:43: The Vulgate specifies duodecim millia ('twelve thousand') drachmas of silver and explicitly adds pro peccatis mortuorum ('for the sins of the dead'), whereas the Greek has 'two thousand' drachmas for a sin offering.
notes.12:45: Native Clementine Vulgate divides Saints.Bible 12:45 across 12:45 and 12:46.
notes.13:2: The Vulgate reads 'five thousand' horsemen, whereas the Greek has 'five thousand three hundred.'
notes.13:4: The Vulgate reads in eodem loco ('in that same place'; so also in v. 5), whereas the Greek names the city of Beroea.
notes.13:7: The Vulgate creates a deliberate wordplay between tali lege ('by such a law') and praevaricatorem legis ('the transgressor of the law'), where the Greek reads 'by such a fate.'
notes.13:24: In the Vulgate, the king appoints Maccabeus himself as commander and ruler (ducem et principem), whereas the Greek states that he left Hegemonides as governor.
notes.13:25: The Vulgate clause indignantes ne forte foedus irrumperent ('being indignant, for fear that perhaps they might violate the covenant') diverges in syntax from the Greek, which states that they were angry at the stipulations and wanted to annul the agreements.
notes.14:1: The Vulgate reads per portam Tripolis ("through the gate of Tripolis"), whereas the Greek reads "into the harbor at Tripolis."
notes.14:2: The Vulgate reads tenuisse regiones adversus Antiochum ("had occupied the regions against Antiochus"), whereas the Greek reports that Demetrius had done away with Antiochus and Lysias.
notes.14:19: The Vulgate reads Theodotium ("Theodotius") and Matthiam ("Matthias"), where the Greek has "Theodotus" and "Mattathias"; giving and receiving right hands is an ancient idiom for pledging peace.
notes.14:33: The Vulgate reads Libero patri ("Father Liber," the Roman deity of wine), where the Greek has "Dionysus."
notes.14:44: The Vulgate reads venit per mediam cervicem ("he came down on the middle of his neck"), whereas the Greek has "in the middle of the empty space" (or "on his flank").
notes.15:30: The Vulgate uniquely describes Judas as "ready in body and soul to die for the citizens" (mori pro civibus paratus erat), whereas the Greek describes him as the chief champion in body and soul who kept his youthful goodwill toward his compatriots.
notes.15:32: The Latin verse has no main verb of its own: ostenso capite... is an ablative absolute and gloriatus est belongs to the relative clause, so the sentence continues with jussit ("ordered") in verse 33.
notes.15:34: Omnes igitur cæli can be construed "all the heavens" (as here) or, taking cæli as genitive with Dominum, "all blessed the Lord of heaven"; the Greek has "all [the people], looking toward heaven, blessed the manifest Lord."
notes.15:36: The Latin text here ends the sentence after "without celebration" and has no equivalent of the Greek specification of the date (the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar, the day before Mordecai's day).
notes.15:37: Native Vulgate 2 Maccabees 15:37 maps to Saints.Bible 15:36b (shifting native 15:38-40 to Saints.Bible 15:37-39).
notes.15:40: The Vulgate epilogue differs markedly from the Greek: it contrasts always drinking wine or water with using them in turn (rather than mixing them), and notes that an account that is "always exacting" (semper exactus) will not please readers.
